# 04. Learning and discovery

A roguelike takes almost everything away when the character dies. What it cannot take away is what the player has learned, and that makes a roguelike, above all, something to be learned. This chapter is about designing for that: deciding what players should come to understand, how the game lets them understand it, and where it should deliberately leave them in the dark.

The talks approach the question from both ends. One group asks how players learn at all: what kinds of skill a roguelike builds, how a generator's output becomes readable rather than noise, how feedback and death teach, what newcomers do not know, and how to onboard without spoiling the discovery. A second group asks what to hide: how much transparency a rule needs, which information to withhold, when mystery is productive, what to do about item identification, how to build investigation into a game, and what happens when the answers end up on a wiki. The speakers broadly agree that learning must be possible from inside the game. Where they part ways is over how much should remain uncertain, and which uncertainty is the point.

## In brief

- What survives permadeath is the player's knowledge, so the progression a roguelike really offers is learning across runs; several independent talks put this at the heart of the genre ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 3:13](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=193); [George Moromisato 2016, 9:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=548); [Tariq et al. 2016, 17:58](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1078); [Jim Shepard 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=339)).
- Treat the difference between novice and expert play as your game's curriculum, and check what players actually learn, because in Gillian Smith's teaching it is almost never the lesson she intended ([bhauth 2020, 6:51](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=411); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:26:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5214); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:17:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4652)).
- Procedural generation pushes players past memorising routes towards learning principles they can generalise, which is the kind of skill a roguelike should be built to teach ([Pandamander 2024, 14:16](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=856); [Andrea Roberts 2019, 7:45](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=465); [John Harris 2016, 27:51](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1671)).
- Randomness can only be learned when its structure is perceptible: when players cannot see how inputs shape output, a generator reads as noise, and flat or streaky randomness teaches patterns that are not there ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:51](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1011); [Isaac Karth 2019, 23:49](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1429); [Max Kreminski 2017, 9:58](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=598); [Evan Debenham 2022, 3:14](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=194); [Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:55](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=595)).
- Feedback teaches best when it arrives close to the decision that caused it; long-term consequences are the hardest thing to teach, so make early warnings and make death explain itself ([Jeff Lait 2025, 5:19](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=319); [Jeff Lait 2025, 7:34](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=454); [Sersa Victory 2022, 7:03](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=423); [Various 2018, 10:55](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=655); [Quinten Konyn 2025, 4:21](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=261)).
- Much of a roguelike's difficulty is genre literacy that veterans no longer notice they carry, so list your game's assumptions and watch newcomers play rather than asking them how they felt ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=324); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 7:07](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=427); [Tabea Iseli 2022, 15:30](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=930); [Darren Grey 2020, 14:31](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=871); [Max Sahin 2025, 1:46](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=106)).
- In a learning game, accessibility means not interfering with learning: teach the unfun foundations briefly, help only players who are visibly stuck, and pace complexity, for example by rarity ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 4:08](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=248); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 8:36](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=516); [Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 13:21](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=801); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=670); [Gavin Verhey 2024, 4:38](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=278)).
- Several designers hold that whatever a player is meant to deduce must be deducible from inside the game, because guesswork is not gameplay and making players look mechanics up in a FAQ is lazy design ([Jim Shepard 2019, 21:19](https://youtu.be/LKCRim02opc?t=1279); [Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955); [Jim Shepard 2017, 32:34](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1954)).
- Uncertainty is a design lever, not a default: decide what to hide, keep the mystery productive by making everything else crystal clear, and make hypotheses cheap to test ([Nic Tringali 2023, 17:51](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1071); [Alexei Pepers 2025, 35:32](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2132); [Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057); [Alexei Pepers 2025, 21:28](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1288)).
- Randomisation only delays spoilers, so pair it with in-game sources of each run's answers and keep the strategy space contingent enough to tip the odds against looking things up ([John Harris 2016, 22:09](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1329); [Zack Johnson 2016, 20:48](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1248); [Jason Grinblat 2016, 9:05](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=545); [Brian Walker 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=280); [Brian Walker 2016, 27:44](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1664)).

## Knowledge is the progression

When a roguelike character dies, almost everything goes with it: the levels, the items, the build. What does not go is what the player has learned ([Jim Shepard 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=339)). Several talks, years apart, put this at the centre of the genre, and it is the right place to start thinking about how your game teaches.

### What survives permadeath

Andrea Roberts calls deep self-directed learning the heart of the roguelike: players discover the underlying rules for themselves, fail, and build the mastery that lets them improvise against whatever the generator produces ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 3:13](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=193)). George Moromisato makes the same point about NetHack by contrast with big-budget games, which he likens to skydiving: you have the experience and you are done. In NetHack any single game matters little; the pleasure is in how good you get, working out combinations and recognising how to escape situations ([George Moromisato 2016, 9:08](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=548)).

Two more talks state the mechanism plainly. In a 2016 lightning talk, a speaker named Dan put it as a business lesson: the only thing you keep between runs is what is in your head, not experience points but actual experience, so progress comes from spotting patterns and not repeating mistakes ([Tariq et al. 2016, 17:58](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1078)). Jim Shepard, talking about metaprogression, argues that the character starts fresh but the player does not: knowledge of monsters, puzzle solutions, static map areas and hidden counters carries over and is itself a form of progression. His example is a player killed by an arrow-shooting centaur who, next time, ducks behind a corridor on sight. Developers cannot stop this, Shepard says, so they should embrace it ([Jim Shepard 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=339)).

> Every game you start fresh with that fresh character, but does the player start fresh? And we know that's not true. — [Jim Shepard 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=339)

Four independent talks converging on one idea is about as strong as the evidence in this bible gets. The practical consequence is that the thing you are really designing is a curriculum. Learning is also slow by construction: because randomness means some elements appear only occasionally, understanding them means meeting them and dying to them, which makes the game harder, as an audience member put it to Shawn Main (Main's own answer was that the appeal for him is the personal story each run creates) ([Shawn Main 2017, 17:02](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1022)). Caves of Qud's developers accept the cost openly: many of the game's huge number of mutation combinations produce characters that simply die, and Jason Grinblat treats that as part of learning the game ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 10:38](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=638)). Learning is also measurable. Phenry Ewing's Monte Carlo model of Cat Burglar included a learning effect taken from test data, with players' success rising each playthrough, so difficulty could be tuned against players who were getting better ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 22:42](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1362)).

### Designers as educators

If the game is a curriculum, the designer is a teacher. Gillian Smith makes this argument directly: if educators are roguelike designers, then roguelike designers are also educators, and they should ask what they want players to learn about the world's underlying systems and how players can shape it, and also what designers can learn from players ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:26:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5214)). She offers a model for a generative space that teaches, using oatmeal toppings: learners need agency to choose (nobody learns from being force-fed bananas), exposure to possibilities they did not know existed (someone has to show them strawberries are an option) and guardrails that keep them from wandering somewhere useless (they still end up with oatmeal) ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:09:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4197)). Mapped onto a roguelike, those are the player's choices, the content the generator surfaces, and the constraints that keep a run coherent.

Smith also brings a warning from her teaching. With ungrading, where students say what they learned and assess themselves, she finds that the most important lesson students take away is almost never the one she meant to teach, and she suggests roguelikes could use the same idea to find out what players are actually learning ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:17:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4652)). Whatever you intend your game to teach, check what it does teach.

### Why players keep coming back to learn

Learning a punishing game has to feel worth it, and the talks offer several accounts of why it does. Pandamander, following Ben Lewis-Evans, points out that dopamine is the neurotransmitter of motivation and anticipation rather than pleasure: it rises while you anticipate a reward and drops back once you get it, so the build-up is the fun part, not the peak ([Pandamander 2024, 2:31](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=151)). Sersa Victory locates that build-up in uncertainty: in traditional roguelikes so much is random (whether the next level is survivable, whether an attack hits, whether an unknown scroll is safe) that the struggle to master uncertainty through careful choices takes centre stage, and players would be bored if they knew the answers ([Sersa Victory 2022, 8:08](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=488)).

Ben McGraw describes the same pull through character building. In Master of Magic, the joy of discovering skill and spell interactions lessened the pain of dying, because he believed he could build his way out of failure; each set of builds taught him enough to want new ones, and meanwhile he got good at the game ([Ben McGraw 2017, 16:25](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=985)). He ties this to Magic: The Gathering's "Johnny" player type, defined by a craving to find combos and discover new interactions, who is drawn to build systems with large design spaces ([Ben McGraw 2017, 17:57](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1077)). Younès Rabii finds a version of the same pleasure in Pokemon Glitch, a corrupted Pokemon: facing situations the original never posed forces players to combine what they already know of the game with creativity, and rediscovering a familiar game is what makes it exciting to explore ([Younès Rabii 2021, 7:58](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=478)).

The structure of the genre helps too. Hannah Blair Salzman argues that randomness, easy task switching and short runs together reduce frustration, because repetitive play feels like small, varied tidbits rather than one long repetitive task; people she spoke to with similar conditions agreed, though she notes it differs for everyone ([Hannah Blair Salzman 2022, 11:02](https://youtu.be/6GSXaM1PTMg?t=662)). Andrew Cedotal adds that tension and relief land most deeply when the anxiety a game creates matches what its audience actually feels; relief is proportional to the irritant ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 23:23](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1403)).

Not every player wants to be optimising, though. Jon Perry explains that UFO 50's Lords of Vicenzo hands players units in a random order (pick from the first three of a queue) precisely so they can relax instead of working out an optimal purchase order; he contrasts Slay the Spire's predictable enemy choices, which suit players who want to think more ([Jon Perry 2025, 41:09](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2469)). Randomness can invite mastery or excuse players from it, and you choose which.

### Giving knowledge somewhere to live

Knowledge does not have to live only in the player's head. Zach and Tarn Adams called Moria's monster memory, which recorded across games how hard a creature hit and what it could do, their favourite part of that game: it persisted knowledge through character deaths and made play feel like exploring a strange planet, and it helped inspire Dwarf Fortress's editable creature files ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 5:56](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=356)). Shepard notes the same thing in Angband, whose monster dictionary stores what you learned so you can look it up later ([Jim Shepard 2017, 6:12](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=372)); the section on making rules readable describes how Angband reveals that knowledge progressively.

Discovery can also be the carrot that pulls the player forward. slashie's Emerald Woods tells the woods' history through documents, magazine articles and video clips in scattered buildings, and puts some animal species only in very specific places, so the player always has a reason to go a bit further ([slashie 2026, 9:11:36](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=33096)). But slashie also reports the limit of this. His exploration sandbox Expedition had sailing, discovering and mapping in place, and still left him asking what players should actually do; his conclusion is that exploration works well alongside other elements but is hard to make the main reason players come back ([slashie 2026, 9:09:23](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32963)).

**In practice.** Write down what your game is meant to teach: which rules, which judgements, which habits. Decide where that knowledge accumulates (the player's head, an in-game record like a monster memory, or both) ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 5:56](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=356)) and make sure discovery is paired with something else to do, rather than being the whole reason to play ([slashie 2026, 9:09:23](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32963)). Then find out, by watching and asking players what they learned, whether the lesson that lands is the one you designed ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:17:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4652)).

## Knowledge, logic and wit: how players come to understand a game

If what the player keeps is knowledge, it helps to be precise about what kinds of knowing roguelike skill involves, and how one kind turns into another.

### Three kinds of skill

John Harris divides game-playing skill into three parts. Knowledge is facts you consciously know, such as that cockatrices turn you to stone, or that you should engrave in the dust with your finger before engrave-testing a wand, since some wand effects are only conclusive when text is already there. Logic is applying those rules to deduce the game state. Wit is intuition, the things you don't know you know: the ability of the friend who wins a new game on the first try ([John Harris 2016, 21:05](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1265)).

The three are not fixed. Harris describes how hidden probabilities pass from one to the next. Suppose one room yields treasure 70% of the time and a horrible monster 30%, and another room mirrors those odds. A player who plays enough first develops a subconscious feeling for which to choose, and later notices and states the rule: chance becomes wit, then knowledge ([John Harris 2016, 25:21](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1521)). This gives you a way to think about hidden numbers in your own game: they are not hidden from a dedicated player, only delayed.

For Harris, the core of roguelike play is in that experiential middle: finding things only experience can teach. He compares it to expert crossword solvers, who learn that a rare letter like the X in "xylophone" constrains its crossing words, and cryptogram solvers, who learn word shapes from length and letter frequency. Both have rules of thumb, but experience builds the real sense of what is possible. He thinks fully achieving this in a game is impossible but worth chasing ([John Harris 2016, 27:51](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1671)).

### Principles, not routes

Three talks converge on what that experience is for. Pandamander borrows a chess term: the first 10 to 15 moves of a game are often memorised "book" openings, but every game eventually reaches a position never recorded, and with memorisation gone the player must generalise from what they have learned. Going out of book, they argue, is the signature move of roguelikes, because each generated map is unique ([Pandamander 2024, 14:16](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=856)). Andrea Roberts makes the same contrast with platformers: you can rehearse a Mario level, but a Spelunky player has no such luxury and must tease apart the game's underlying principles and build a palette of reactions. Strong roguelike players come to know a game's design as well as its designers, and Roundguard's beta players sometimes taught her implications of her own design ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 7:45](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=465)). Harris's crossword sense is the same thing from the other side ([John Harris 2016, 27:51](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1671)). Generation is what forces the learning to be about principles rather than routes.

Roundguard shows what principled play looks like in the moment. Roberts walks through a shot: she is certain of the first bounce, confident of the next, then reasons in zones of likelihood (probably the middle, where health potions are; possibly left, toward hard-hitting orcs, which matters at half health; unlikely right, where mana potions would be wasted at full mana) and decides it is a good turn to spend skills ([Andrea Roberts 2019, 4:22](https://youtu.be/2BHfpAF76J8?t=262)). That is knowledge, logic and wit working together on a physics system nobody can memorise.

### Chaos is the feeling of not yet understanding

Joel Clark offers a useful definition: chaos in a game is not objective disorder but a personal experience, the discomfort of struggling to understand something. The same system feels more chaotic to one person than another depending on what they understand, and design can be seen as repeatedly exposing players to chaos and then showing them a path through it ([Joel Clark 2020, 6:18](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=378)). His everyday example is a new boss with unfamiliar attacks: unpredictable until you get hit once or twice and lose a few times, after which you recognise the patterns and it stops being chaotic ([Joel Clark 2020, 7:09](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=429)).

> Chaos is discomfort caused by trying to understand something. — [Joel Clark 2020, 6:18](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=378)

Clark's evidence from Blaseball, a messy, improvised and random game that many people nonetheless keep up with, is that players have a higher threshold for confusion and learning than designers assume, because making sense of things is rewarding; it felt most chaotic when the community was struggling to interpret new information ([Joel Clark 2020, 16:23](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=983)). Jongwoo Kim saw the same arc in The Shrouded Isle: players first acted on their own morality and emotions, but after about one season adopted an "inner tyrant" mindset as they learned what the systems reward ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)). Kim draws the line that matters elsewhere in the same Q&A: if the systems were completely random and opaque, that would be frustration without a purpose ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)). Confusion is tolerable when there is something to understand.

### The skill gap as a design lens

bhauth offers a practical way to see what your game teaches: compare what new players do with what very good players do. That difference is what the game teaches, and in some sense the essence of its gameplay. In Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS), new players don't retreat upstairs or identify consumables; the game teaches planning ahead for future resource needs rather than looping explore, attack, level up. In his fork bcrawl he made identify scrolls always identified to encourage players to identify things, though he is unsure how well it worked ([bhauth 2020, 6:51](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=411)).

The gap is not one-dimensional. Tarn Adams notes that character skills which reveal clues, such as tracking footprints in Dwarf Fortress, are tricky because players learn to read the clues themselves after seeing enough; he accepts that as just getting better at the game, while the character still matters ([Tarn Adams 2018, 21:38](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1298)). Gavin Verhey reports that in Magic drafting, public win-rate data is useful directionally but card strength is contextual, so drafting purely by numbers yields incoherent decks; both data-driven newer players and intuition-driven veterans succeed ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 28:00](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1680)), which is Harris's knowledge and wit as two routes across the gap. And at the far end, expert communities build shared knowledge of their own: Nat Alison describes Sudoku constructors devising new kinds of deduction a computer would brute-force but a human can solve logically, and building a shared meta-game of theorems on each other's work ([Nat Alison 2023, 10:16](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=616)).

### The far end of mastery

What happens when the gap is crossed? Kawa describes conducts (self-imposed restrictions such as never eating meat) as what players invent once they have mastered a game and start treating its mechanics as a toy, asking whether removing a mechanic or doing things a certain way is harder, more interesting or tests different skills ([Kawa 2019, 19:06](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1146)). Tim Keenan observes that new players value variety within a run while experienced players increasingly favour variety between runs, which is why heavily constrained modes like daily runs appeal to veterans ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:40:47](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31247)). And Harris, a multiple NetHack ascender, admits that despite its reputation NetHack's depth is finite: after reading the wiki many times you learn everything in it, which reduced his interest ([John Harris 2016, 4:31](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=271)).

**In practice.** Watch a novice and an expert play your game and write down how their behaviour differs. That list is your curriculum ([bhauth 2020, 6:51](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=411)). For each item, ask whether a player can cross the gap from inside the game: is there a pattern to notice, enough repetition to notice it, and a moment where the hidden rule can become a conscious one? Then plan for the players who finish crossing: constrained modes and room for self-imposed challenges extend a game's life after its knowledge is exhausted ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:40:47](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31247); [Kawa 2019, 19:06](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=1146)).

## Reading the generator: making randomness learnable

A player can only learn from procedural content whose structure they can perceive. If the rules behind a generator are invisible, its output is noise, and noise teaches nothing, or teaches the wrong thing.

### Legible generators

Emilia Lazer-Walker found this out on Computational Flaneur, a poem-reading companion for walks. Rain, walking speed, time of day and nearby people originally all changed the poems, but nobody expects a poetry companion to respond to how fast they walk, so the effects were invisible; she cut the inputs down to simple GPS regions (by the water, you hear water poems). Her summary: when players cannot model how inputs shape the output, it is indistinguishable from randomness. Roguelikes, she notes, do better because their mechanics, like water making surfaces slippery, are understandable metaphors for the real world ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:51](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1011)).

> Black box emulation is indistinct from randomness. — [Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 16:51](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1011)

Isaac Karth gives the most complete account of how players read generators. His "aesthetic locus" lens asks whether a player is focused on how something was made (the generator's structure) or on what it does (the surface). As players become familiar with a generator their attention naturally drifts toward structure, but in roguelikes the individual details matter so much (a lowercase d is not a capital D dragon) that attention stays on the surface, which he thinks is one reason procedural generation works so well in the genre ([Isaac Karth 2019, 11:27](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=687)). Players can still learn the structure indirectly. Minecraft places diamonds by rules, always in clusters and at particular depths, so players learn to dig down to a certain depth with the right pickaxe without knowing where any particular diamond is ([Isaac Karth 2019, 13:05](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=785)). NetHack uses its sound messages to let you hear features you have not yet found, hinting at what kind of level you are on; Karth lists unique room shapes and scattered clues as other ways to warn players before they reach a special room ([Isaac Karth 2019, 30:37](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1837)). His general advice is to foreground causality. NetHack tracks the source of every instance of damage so its death message can name the killer, and he suggests extending the idea to the generator itself: give rooms made by a particular technique a distinctive style, such as a floor pattern, so players can learn the association ([Isaac Karth 2019, 23:49](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1429)).

Younès Rabii frames the whole problem as one of interpretation: a slash and a green g become "I hold a sword and a goblin is to my right", and Dwarf Fortress screenshots that look like keyboard mashing yield stories with plot twists. If player interpretation is what makes roguelike stories possible, designing a roguelike can be seen as shaping player interpretation ([Younès Rabii 2020, 2:00](https://youtu.be/s6Kxh_Zyiqs?t=120)).

### Expectation first, then surprise

Learnable structure is also what makes surprise possible. Martin Pichlmair, whose PhD was on the topic, argues that rule-bound randomness creates delight because the player builds an expectation of the outcome, and the gap between expectation and the actual, not fully predictable result produces surprise; fully random output would create no expectations at all ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 15:24](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=924)). Matt Carney finds the same structure in Terry Riley's minimalist piece In C, where repetition lets you learn the rules and anticipate while leaving room for something new, and connects it to a paper on system suspense by Jason Grinblat, Alexei Pepers and others ([Matt Carney 2026, 26:49](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=1609)), an idea that gets its own section later in this chapter.

Two practical consequences follow. First, expectations take time to build. Max Kreminski points out that players need to learn a generator's baseline before they can recognise an exceptional event, and that true randomness misleads early: a random sequence of the digits 0 to 4 contains long runs of only one or two values, and a player whose first experience is such a run may conclude the game always does the same thing ([Max Kreminski 2017, 9:58](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=598)). Second, patterns must exist before they can be broken. Alex Byaly's causal-graph generator produces correlated creatures, so players learn stereotypes; a few of his goats do eat mice, and someone who assumes no mouse-eater is a goat will occasionally be surprised, a surprise that could not happen in pattern-free data ([Alex Byaly 2022, 22:43](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1363)). Byaly proposes, though he has not yet used it in a real game, holding generated correlations fixed across runs or for a period such as a week, so players can learn them, discuss them and plan around them before the game rotates to a new version ([Alex Byaly 2022, 25:03](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1503)).

Discovering that a pattern was intended is itself rewarding. Nat Alison notes the worry that a striking pattern is mere coincidence, and the pleasure when it turns out not to be: roguelike synergies that first look like flukes were placed by developers for players to find ([Nat Alison 2024, 21:17](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=1277)).

### How randomness miseducates

The flip side is that people find patterns whether or not they exist. The creators of Rogue recall players who believed an algorithm made some games "scroll heavy"; no such system existed, and the speaker took from it a lesson in how people personify algorithms and build a world around them ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:55](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=595)). Max Hawkins, who let a randomiser choose where he went, found himself reading meaning into pure noise, as when a random destination for discussing the end of a project sent him and his partner to a pet cemetery ([Max Hawkins 2019, 16:03](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=963)).

Evan Debenham connects this to how you roll numbers. With a uniform range, a maximum or minimum roll feels special but is no rarer than any other value, and two maximum rolls in a row feel exceptional; over time players come to believe the game is working for or against them when it is not, and large ranges make the variance worse ([Evan Debenham 2022, 3:14](https://youtu.be/kaojiu9syPE?t=194)). Shawn Main points out that this misreading can serve the player's ego: randomness gives players something to blame for a loss, which in Magic means many complaints about bad draws are a convenient scapegoat rather than the real reason they lost. Main sees that emotional protection as genuinely valuable ([Shawn Main 2017, 11:17](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=677)), but it is also a lesson the player did not learn.

**In practice.**

- Keep inputs to a generator few and legible enough that a player could guess how they affect the output (Lazer-Walker).
- Give generator techniques a visible signature, such as a room shape or floor pattern, and let players sense structure before they reach it, as NetHack's sounds do (Karth).
- Surface causes: say what hit the player, and from where, in messages and death screens (Karth).
- Prefer shaped distributions to flat ones where you want players to strategise, so extreme results are actually rare (Debenham).
- Establish a baseline before you show exceptions, and watch for early random streaks that teach a false rule (Kreminski).
- Consider keeping some correlations stable long enough, across runs or for a week, that players can learn and share them (Byaly).

## Feedback loops and the lessons of death

Most of what a roguelike teaches, it teaches through consequences. That works well when the consequence follows the decision closely. It works badly when it doesn't.

### The long-loop problem

Jeff Lait names the problem: games are good at short feedback loops, where you learn quickly from mistakes, but long-term consequences are among the hardest things to express, and players who fail a long loop often don't recognise it as a loop at all and just call the game bad ([Jeff Lait 2025, 5:19](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=319)). His examples are familiar. New NetHack players often starve because the first time they think about food is when "Hungry" appears on screen, which is too late: food has to be managed from the start, by picking up rations and eating corpses, and players who don't conclude the game is impossible ([Jeff Lait 2025, 12:39](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=759)). In his own survival 7DRL (a game made in a seven-day roguelike jam), each run is a new island with the same rules, tools and systems and no stated goals. Players learned to make a campfire, but not the longer loop of stopping every so often to warm up while exploring; they kept walking through snow, or lit a fire and left after a turn or two, and froze ([Jeff Lait 2025, 28:35](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1715)).

Lait's model of doing it well is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which teaches through clear signposting, early feedback, quick deaths that return you near the decision point, and nested loops that scaffold from short cycles up to meta-level mechanics. He was struck that he never had to save ([Jeff Lait 2025, 7:34](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=454)).

> Games seem good working short feedback loops where we learn quickly from mistakes, but anything long-term players walk out and fail to learn. — [Jeff Lait 2025, 5:19](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=319)

### Should everything be learnable?

Here Lait takes a contrarian position. If games train us to expect that everything is learnable through short, enjoyable feedback loops, he argues, we lose the ability to learn things in the world that lack such loops; there is no reason everything we need to learn fits the pattern our brains evolved ([Jeff Lait 2025, 9:30](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=570)). He accepts that difficulty walls and hidden growth hurt review scores, but says designers should be willing to break those rules when they intend to ([Jeff Lait 2025, 14:21](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=861)), and concludes that while most games should stay easy to learn, hard-to-learn games that force unguided meta-learning are as valid a design space as hard-to-master ones ([Jeff Lait 2025, 29:16](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1756)).

The mainstream case runs the other way. Sersa Victory, drawing on a widely cited definition of meaningful play, sets out three conditions for a choice to feel meaningful: the player knows what she is choosing, gets clear feedback on the immediate result, and can see how it affected the longer-term outcome; a player who feels nothing she does matters becomes bored and frustrated ([Sersa Victory 2022, 7:03](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=423)). Shawn Main warns that heavy outcome randomness, as in poker, obscures skill: a newcomer can make the correct play, lose, and conclude it was wrong, so players are rewarded for bad decisions, punished for good ones, and learn the wrong lessons ([Shawn Main 2017, 10:18](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=618)). The two positions are not strictly opposed, since Lait agrees most games should be easy to learn. The choice depends on whether learning the long loop unaided is the experience you want to offer, and on whether you accept that many players will leave before they get there.

### What novices get wrong

Several talks describe the same handful of novice failures, and they are the lessons feedback most needs to deliver. bhauth says new DCSS players use consumables in combat too rarely and too late; the game teaches them to slow down and consider all their options when things go wrong ([bhauth 2020, 7:50](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=470)). Josh Grams saw players of his turn-based space-flight game make real-time mistakes, accelerating too fast and panicking into walls, until someone told them to take their hands off the keyboard and they realised they could stop and think ([Josh Grams 2020, 7:38](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=458)). Andrea Interguglielmi found that Nauticrawl's players did not realise there were turns at all, and rushed their moves to escape pursuers, generating heat and noise that made things worse ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 12:16](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=736)). Quinten Konyn, dissecting one of his own deaths, notes the mirror image: players hoard resources against obviously dangerous, highlighted foes but underestimate familiar, weak-seeming ones. Having already killed five cobalts, he did not think the sixth could kill him ([Quinten Konyn 2025, 8:35](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=515)). In each case the player misreads time or threat, and the game must make the cost of that misreading visible.

### The morgue: closing the loop after death

The roguelike's traditional answer to long consequences is the post-mortem. Kawa expands the old term "morgue" (originally a printout of a dead character) to cover everything between a character's death and the player's choice to quit or try again, and gives it three functions: conveying lore and tone, improving play, and fuelling storytelling. Player discussion between games is part of the same extra-ludic space and forms a game's culture ([Various 2018, 10:55](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=655)). How much detail it needs depends on the game: DCSS records everything about a character so players can study how they could have done better (Kawa's mid-game morgue would have run to 41 pages, and public servers keep morgue folders anyone can read), while Crypt of the NecroDancer shows only the last twelve beats, which suits a small game ([Various 2018, 14:40](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=880)).

Konyn shows what a detailed morgue makes possible. A DCSS morgue file records the messages leading up to death and an ASCII snapshot of the map with a list of visible creatures. By highlighting every damage message (more exclamation marks means more damage) and using the creature list to disambiguate the colourless map, he identified three attackers: an orc warrior with a reach-two glaive, an orc high priest attacking from afar, and a cobalt blast miner whose range-four cannon hit hardest ([Quinten Konyn 2025, 4:21](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=261)). The notes and skills sections then showed an unused option: his character's "heal other" ability, boosted by high Invocations skill, had earlier pacified an orc warlord and might have neutralised the killer. He concludes he held back for fear of spending god favour and because he underestimated the enemy; his own judgement was the murderer ([Quinten Konyn 2025, 7:10](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=430)). That is a long loop closed after the fact: the morgue makes the cause of death legible enough that the lesson lands.

Causal information does not have to wait for a morgue file: as noted under reading the generator, NetHack's death message can name the killer because the game tracks the source of every damage instance ([Isaac Karth 2019, 23:49](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1429)). And DCSS players can go further, querying aggregate data across servers; Alan Malloy queried recent games entering the optional Elven Halls by experience level and the share who died there, and concluded that around level 19 is a reasonable time to go, while noting small samples and imperfect queries ([Alan Malloy 2017, 17:08](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1028)).

Death records shape play as well as reflect it. A 2018 lightning-talk speaker argues that recording player-described deaths encourages healthy metagaming: when death is foreseeable, players act in character to make it dramatic, which he finds more fun than thinking tactically ([Various 2018, 26:42](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1602)). Players also make their own records. Florence Smith Nicholls found players of Nothing Beside Remains drawing maps or taking screenshots, records that scaffolded their interpretations and worked like keepsakes ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2025, 7:33](https://youtu.be/9kqvF2TqxLo?t=453)). Mike Cook, who has been playing Smith Nicholls's keepsake game Bleed Map (you draw and annotate a map of what you do in a video game), suggests designers do this while playing their own game to notice what they are and aren't paying attention to, though he has not yet tried it on one of his ([Mike Cook 2026, 20:10](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1210)).

**In practice.** For each important long-term habit in your game, ask when the player first gets evidence that it matters. If the first signal is a warning that comes too late, like "Hungry", add an earlier one, or a short loop that rehearses the habit ([Jeff Lait 2025, 12:39](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=759)). Return the player close to the decision that failed, as Lait's Clair Obscur example does ([Jeff Lait 2025, 7:34](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=454)). Make death explain itself: name the killer and where the damage came from, keep the last messages and the map, and size the morgue to the game ([Isaac Karth 2019, 23:49](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1429); [Various 2018, 14:40](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=880)). If you deliberately leave a loop unguided, as Lait argues you sometimes should, do it knowing the cost ([Jeff Lait 2025, 29:16](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1756)).

## Who is learning: genre literacy, player types and playtesting

Much of what makes a roguelike hard is knowledge veterans carry without noticing. Andrea Roberts puts it directly: because roguelikes are about learning, experienced players arrive with expectations that make the game easier for them, so so much of the difficulty lies in what you already understand. Testing those assumptions was the key to Roundguard's onboarding ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=324)).

### Genre literacy

The assumptions go deeper than designers expect. Roundguard's team took trading damage and managing health across a run as basics, but early playtests showed newcomers did not grasp that enemies hit back on contact, or that health must last a whole run; in many games players avoid most damage and are healed after every encounter ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 7:07](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=427)). Tabea Iseli calls this game literacy, covering both roguelike conventions and basic vocabulary like "touching an enemy hurts". Nothing about a cute turtle says it kills on touch; players know from other games. Making Grimoire Groves non-violent wiped out much of that literacy, so players had to relearn what contact does and what ends the game, a lengthy process that can be unfun for players and developers alike ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 15:30](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=930)).

> If you have year zero game literacy, how would you know touching the turtle kills you? — [Tabea Iseli 2022, 15:30](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=930)

Iseli says the hardest part of the project was not inventing non-violent mechanics but balancing reliance on literacy against subverting it; because non-violence was already a big subversion, the team minimised others ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 17:29](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1049)). One technique was to borrow literacy from another genre: roguelike loot drops made plants look stabbed with guts spilling out, so the team swapped in farming games' button-press harvesting ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 21:22](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1282)).

Literacy from the wrong genre causes its own failures. Darren Grey describes FTL's giant alien spiders event as a "hero trap": players from standard RPGs send crew to help and get punished, because heroism is not how you survive in roguelikes, and newcomers who say yes to every quest die a lot ([Darren Grey 2020, 14:31](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=871)). Likewise trap detection and status effects are optional extras in a standard RPG but core requirements in a roguelike, so players who misread the genre neglect them; Grey argues for framing up front how the game should be approached ([Darren Grey 2020, 19:08](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1148)).

Even experienced players miss what their literacy says cannot happen. Courtney Liessen reports that Reality Break players see the lightning-bolt icon next to an item's ship-class requirement and still don't realise they can shrink the item instead of buying a bigger ship; rule-breaking options need clearer communication ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 10:44](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=644)). Into the Breach's deployment turn is commonly misread as random and information-free (Netflix QA filed it as a bug during the mobile port), although players can place melee mechs close, ranged ones far and stay out of web range; Matthew Davis calls this a failure to have the information ready for the player rather than a difference of design taste ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 5:40](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=340)). And expectations form before play: Alexei Pepers notes that marketing, reviews, art style, genre and team size all set them, so players are not a blank slate, and designers can exploit this; a Caves of Qud achievement about wearing your own severed face primes curiosity before play begins ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 14:19](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=859)).

### First contact

The first minutes are where literacy gaps hurt most. Ben McGraw describes a roguelike's first five minutes as choosing a build and dying several times: veterans wonder what this game adds over all their other deaths, and newcomers unfamiliar with the genre's lethality may head straight for the refund page ([Ben McGraw 2017, 4:01](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=241)). Stripping away conventions can open the door instead. Lee Tusman, without a D&D or RPG background and put off by memorising many keys and managing inventories, was drawn in by Cosmic Crown, a one-dimensional roguelike in which you move forward one or two spaces, because the simplicity let him focus on understanding the system, which still produced surprising emergent mechanics ([Lee Tusman 2020, 3:08](https://youtu.be/-e4gF_SKWPk?t=188)).

### Different appetites for discovery

Players also differ in how much discovery they want. Lisa Brown uses Quantic Foundry's Gamer Motivation Profile (six primary motivations, each split into two, scored as percentiles, so a very low score is as strong a preference as a very high one) to explain why particular roguelikes stick with particular players ([Lisa Brown 2020, 6:27](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=387)). Her own low discovery score means she prefers fully exposed rulesets, such as Slay the Spire showing enemy intent and Loot Rascals explaining its combat maths; randomness is fine if it sits inside rules she can learn up front. She suspects that as a professional designer, exploring unknown rules feels like work ([Lisa Brown 2020, 24:23](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1463)). Christine Tomlinson, on a panel about roguelites, adds that some players want challenge and to prove they can beat the developer, while others want to relax and explore characters and stories, which is one reason genre mash-ups proliferate ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 37:40](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2260)). A game that hides its rules for the joy of discovery will lose some players for exactly that reason.

### How you find out

You cannot see your own assumptions, so you need players. Santiago Zapata learned this on Fusion Abyss: he refused an automap in its huge dark levels, believing getting lost was good, and almost no one was willing to wander for two hours looking for a single stairway tile. His lesson is that you have to listen sometimes if you want to make a game someone else will play ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 21:17](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1277)). Brian Cronin describes the payoff of playtesting extensively: new players ask how something works and the next screen answers them, so the game seems to read their minds, because he had already read many other people's minds in earlier tests ([Brian Cronin 2025, 8:22](https://youtu.be/Kh9m-ixeqec?t=502)).

What you ask matters. Max Sahin warns that asking players how they feel about a menu yields little, because people are bad at naming their experience and good interviewing is an expensive skill ([Max Sahin 2025, 1:46](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=106)). He also cautions that general game research transfers poorly: research on meaning comes mostly from MMORPGs and social, narrative play, so applying it to roguelikes can leave you worse off ([Max Sahin 2025, 4:03](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=243)), and findings such as people valuing digital goods less than physical ones (except in games) are muddied further by permadeath ([Max Sahin 2025, 2:56](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=176)).

**In practice.** List the conventions your game assumes, down to "enemies hurt" and "health carries over" ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 5:24](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=324)). For each, decide whether to rely on it, teach it, or subvert it, and keep the number of subversions small ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 17:29](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1049)). Then watch newcomers play, rather than asking them how they felt ([Max Sahin 2025, 1:46](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=106)), and treat every misreading as a missing piece of information.

## Teaching without interfering: onboarding, tutorials and complexity curves

If learning is the point of the game, then teaching it badly can take away the thing players came for. The talks converge on an approach: teach the foundations that aren't fun to discover, catch players who are stuck, pace complexity, and otherwise stay out of the way ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 8:36](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=516); [Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 13:21](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=801); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=670); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 4:08](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=248)).

### Accessibility means not interfering

Andrea Roberts started Roundguard's accessibility work assuming she should make the game easier or add more tutorials, and changed her mind: making a roguelike accessible should mean not interfering with learning. That means not interrupting players who are about to figure something out, trusting them, giving them room to experiment, and avoiding grind-to-win mechanics that create a false sense of progress, so players feel they won through their own learning ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 4:08](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=248)).

> I am trying to encourage learning, and more than anything, I am trying not to interfere with learning. — [Andrea Roberts 2020, 4:08](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=248)

Caelyn Sandel approaches the same question from Caves of Qud's opening. A new player's intended experience fits in a corner of the main menu; random characters would be a bad first experience, there is no build library yet, attribute screens read as D&D jargon, and dozens of mutations must be read without knowing which to take, all before the game shows its strengths of mood, writing and atmosphere ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 4:49](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=289)). Her conclusion is not that the game should be easier: up-front complexity asks new players for more investment, so the game must make that investment pay off and make continuing to try fun, and developers should watch for the knots that slow players down ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 19:51](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1191)).

### The toolkit

**Short tutorials for the unfun foundations.** Roundguard first tried a pop-in tutorial character inside a full procedural run, but heroes, skills, varied monsters and status effects were too much at once. The team made a short, step-by-step tutorial at the start that teaches only that enemies hit back and that potions heal. Roberts concluded these basics are not the fun part, so teaching them does not spoil learning ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 8:36](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=516)). Leif Bloomquist's multiplayer Commodore 64 roguelike makes its first level a tutorial of simple tasks, because its explicit attack command (which attacks with every carried weapon) is an unusual mechanic ([Leif Bloomquist 2018, 17:58](https://youtu.be/Y0K-e83wYnQ?t=1078); [Leif Bloomquist 2019, 15:00](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=900)). The first Shiren the Wanderer includes Fei's Problems, non-random puzzle scenarios that work as a tutorial and are fun on their own; solving one at the start of a run grants a random item for that journey, as John Harris describes ([John Harris 2024, 14:36](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=876)).

**Safety nets that trigger only for strugglers.** Most Roundguard players embraced skills after a brief introduction, so the tutorial character reappears only if a player goes a couple of boards without using them ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 9:55](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=595)). Nauticrawl goes further. When it detects repeated deaths, Andrea Interguglielmi's game starts runs with a diegetic "safety lock" check that teaches one mechanic at a time (battery, stealth, hull or turns). For turns, it places a creature next to the player and a radio broadcast tells pilots to stay still, because nothing moves until you move; if the player dies anyway, the next restart teaches another mechanic, and he reports that it worked ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 13:21](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=801)). Both teach only the players who need it, which keeps everyone else's discovery intact.

**The premise as tutorial.** Nauticrawl gives the player only a premise: a stolen machine they were never allowed to touch, so pushing every button to learn the controls is the opening puzzle, an idea taken from The Room; as the machine becomes familiar, the game fades into dungeon-crawl exploration ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 2:23](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=143)). Chogue, Jonathan Lessard and Pippin Barr's chess roguelike, opens on a plain board where the black king leaves after the player's first move; chess players already know what to do, and the missing king draws them toward the stairs with no text at all ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 1:08](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=68)). Bad News, a live-performed roguelike, opens with a fixed scene in which a mortician character acts as a guide, asking the player to explain the job and helping devise a cover story, so players get used to role-playing before they enter the town ([Bad News team 2016, 50:22](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=3022)).

**Quests that give lost players a direction.** Kristen Yu observes that in high-agency games like Animal Crossing players can feel lost, and quests give them directed goals that make them interact with systems until they can set goals of their own ([Kristen Yu 2021, 13:41](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=821)). Caelyn Sandel taught Caves of Qud's early game twice, the second time through a quest. Her Twine story A Hindren's Guide to Qud taught early-game tricks, such as healing with witchwood bark, having enough armour before moving on, and which enemies to flee, and got her hired onto the team ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 12:12](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=732)). Her later survival-guide mod turns the lessons into a quest delivered by an in-world Hindren character ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 15:18](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=918)).

**Curating the first experience.** Shawn Main notes that first plays shape a player's sense of a random game's difficulty, so a digital game should curate early content so the first action never feels like it screwed the player over ([Shawn Main 2017, 25:36](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1536)). Josh Grams found in playtests that binding the exit stairs to W meant new players pressing W to accelerate lost immediately; he disabled the first level's exit so you cannot lose off the bat ([Josh Grams 2020, 5:33](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=333)).

**Companions as teachers.** Tyriq Plummer learned from Catacomb Kids that people tolerate failure and difficulty better when they have someone to fail with, and a partner can teach mechanics hands-on rather than leaving newcomers to wiki pages ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 6:34](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=394)).

### Pacing complexity

Teaching once is not enough if the game then shows everything at once. Two talks converge on the same mechanism from Magic: The Gathering. Gavin Verhey explains that Magic uses rarity to control reading load: commons are simpler and make up most of each pack, so players mostly process simple cards and learn the complex rares as they take them or see them pass around the table ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 4:38](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=278)). Dan DiIorio borrowed this "New World Order" for Luck be a Landlord: complex symbols are uncommon or rarer, only commons appear at the start of a run, and rarity chances rise gradually after the first few choices, giving a complexity curve analogous to a difficulty curve ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=670)). If your game drafts or offers random rewards, rarity is a ready-made dial for complexity.

Gating works for whole systems too. UFO 50's Mini and Max originally let players shrink to the microscopic scale immediately; Jon Perry realised holding it back would make it a mind-blowing reveal and reduce overwhelm in an already overwhelming game ([Jon Perry 2025, 15:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=906)). Ezra Szanton, who once dismissed explicit synergy callouts as uninteresting, now sees them as essential for new players: Slay the Spire's Perfected Strike names Strike cards outright, Inflame links to attacks through Strength, and Acrobatics with zero-cost Slice is a synergy found only through play; experts can ignore the obvious ones ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 17:11](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1031)). Choice frequency is part of the same budget: Sersa Victory warns that too many choice prompts, especially frequent dilemmas, overload the player and break flow, and that density must be tuned by playtesting, more art than science ([Sersa Victory 2022, 30:28](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1828)).

Against all of this stands Perry's own UFO 50, which he says intentionally overwhelms players, unlike his board games where he carefully manages cognitive load; the team talked openly about overwhelm being part of the point ([Jon Perry 2025, 42:29](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2549)). Even there, he still gated the microscopic scale. Overwhelm can be a deliberate aesthetic, but it is a choice, not a default.

### When discoverability fails

bhauth describes the cost of getting this wrong in DCSS: it has poor discoverability and little guidance toward good strategies, so a new player who keeps dying early with melee characters never sees most of its content, and people can play for years without learning useful features. Watching a good player on YouTube teaches more than the manual or tutorial ([bhauth 2020, 19:51](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1191)). He has considered official video tutorials per archetype and unlockable mid-game character saves showing how good players build, though he has not implemented them ([bhauth 2020, 21:01](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1261)). NetHack has an accidental version of the second idea: its developer debug "wizard mode" gives unlimited wishes and lets you refuse death, and commentators recommend it for exploring late-game content without the skill to reach it ([Adeon 2017, 1:08:33](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=4113)).

**In practice.**

- Teach explicitly only what is foundational and not fun to discover (enemies hit back, potions heal), and do it briefly, at the start.
- Detect struggle (skills unused for a few boards, repeated deaths) and teach only those players, one mechanic at a time, ideally inside the fiction.
- Let the premise or the first screen pose the first puzzle, and make sure the first action cannot lose the game.
- Gate complexity by rarity or progress, call out the obvious synergies, and tune how often you ask for decisions.
- If your game overwhelms on purpose, decide that deliberately.
- Give players a route to deep content they may never reach unaided, whether worked examples of strong builds or a sandbox mode.
- Otherwise, stay out of the way of a player who is about to work something out.

## Making the rules readable: transparency, common sense and in-world cues

If a roguelike is something to be learned, then whatever the player is meant to deduce has to be deducible from inside the game. That does not mean every number must be printed on screen: Voyageur shows every trait that matters without showing exactly how it matters ([Bruno Dias 2016, 16:08](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=968)). The talks describe four different ways of making a rule knowable: lean on what the player already knows about the world, show the rule through the world itself, state it outright, or expose part of it and let the player infer the rest ([George Moromisato 2016, 14:33](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=873); [Mark R Johnson 2019, 7:18](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=438); [Bruno Dias 2016, 16:08](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=968); [Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 31:50](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1910)). The subsections below take them in turn, and a game can use all four, choosing mechanic by mechanic.

### Common sense and the world as a teacher

The cheapest teacher is knowledge the player brings with them. George Moromisato credits NetHack with avoiding spoiler-dependence by making interactions behave as everyday knowledge predicts: dragons resist fire, a dipped scroll gets wet, a dipped sword rusts. Its developers worked to make things a player expected to work actually work. He also names the limit of the approach. In Transcendence, his science-fiction game, nobody knows whether plasma bolts bounce off magnetic shields, so common sense has nothing to grip and he has had to adapt ([George Moromisato 2016, 14:33](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=873)). The further your setting is from daily life, the less of this free teaching you get.

A second in-world strategy is to let the player read the world by looking at it. Mark R Johnson wants Ultima Ratio Regum's generated cultures to be learned from observable cues rather than from a message announcing which culture an NPC belongs to. Each culture and religion has its own clothing style, varying with wealth, and building types share features across cultures so that a player arriving in a new city can still recognise a house, a shop or a church ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 7:18](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=438)).

> The player should be able to learn a lot and reason a lot about the world simply by looking at it and making sense of it. — [Mark R Johnson 2019, 7:18](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=438)

Jeremy Rose supplies the caveat. A realistic simulation such as Cataclysm invites players to reason from real-world knowledge, but the ways it simplifies reality are not obvious, so players are left with constant questions: would a garage have an arc welder, could a book or a laptop teach you to build one from microwave parts, how dangerous is a giant slug? Those questions are what drove him to build his external guide to the game ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 7:25](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=445)). Common sense is a promise; once you make it, every place your simulation breaks it becomes a trap.

### Explicit transparency

The opposite strategy is to state the rules. Bruno Dias describes a design contract in Voyageur: the game never tracks hidden state, and every trait that influences an outcome is visible to the player, even if exactly how it influences the outcome is not ([Bruno Dias 2016, 16:08](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=968)). That split is worth noting. You can show *what matters* without showing the formula.

Jongwoo Kim gives the fairness argument for this kind of transparency, even in a game built on hidden information. In The Shrouded Isle, outcomes are unpredictable, but consistent rules sit underneath and an inquiry system lets the player reveal immediately why someone failed; that means of finding out is what keeps the hidden information from being the purposeless frustration of a random, opaque system. He would seed more revealed information at the start for an easier mode ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)). Jim Shepard makes the same point about relationship systems: if the player must woo an NPC, the game has to make clear what that NPC wants, because guesswork is not gameplay. His counter-example is an NPC who rejects flowers because their mother died of "floweritis", an arbitrary failure the player could never have foreseen ([Jim Shepard 2019, 21:19](https://youtu.be/LKCRim02opc?t=1279)).

Several games show how to build transparency in without dumping everything on screen at once:

- **Progressive recall.** Erik Osheim and Robert Au describe Angband moving towards transparency: it shows damage dealt and wand failure rates, and it reveals a monster's spells, their frequency and their damage progressively as you meet it more often. You still do not know a new monster's spells on first meeting ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 12:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=747)).
- **A knowledge menu.** Angband also added beginner aids: a birth screen with exact race and class stat bonuses, optional sensible starting equipment instead of money, and a knowledge menu that tracks your home, store contents and identified flavours, so you can see where you stand in the identification mini-game from anywhere in the dungeon ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 14:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=867)).
- **Stats and descriptions in the game.** Eric Billingsley counts it among Brogue's strengths that it tells the player what monsters and equipment can do and shows the stats, so players do not need external sources ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 8:57](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=537)). Brian Walker describes how Brogue spends a full line of what he calls very precious screen real estate on flavour text: whenever you step on terrain, the line says what the character sees, hears or feels, and moving the cursor over a glyph describes it. The aim is that for really powerful effects the player gets a clue before it explodes on them ([Brian Walker 2016, 28:56](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1736)).
- **An internal encyclopedia.** Kes notes that older roguelikes such as NetHack carry an internal database of monster and item entries for looking up unfamiliar things, often using real literary quotes ([Kes 2023, 6:03](https://youtu.be/PvMJY8qtmc8?t=363)).
- **Hints as an object.** Cataclysm contains an in-game Hitchhiker's Guide book that gives a random hint from the game's hints file when read; Rose would like his external guide integrated so that an item's page could pop up from inside the game ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 28:54](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1734)).

### Hint without spoiling

Between common sense and an explicit statement lies the partial cue: enough to send the player in the right direction, not enough to replace the discovery. Thomas Biskup describes how Ultimate ADOM replaces ADOM's hundred keys with one context-sensitive "fiddle with the environment" key that offers whatever is reasonably possible. Asked whether streamlining would kill ADOM's charm (wiping mud from your eyes, plugging your ears with beeswax against a banshee), he says items will get suggestive descriptions, such as "sticky, gluey", rather than spoilers, and that the key's detection of possible actions lets players discover them by accident ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 37:26](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=2246)). The same team removed a pure chance element: after a roguelike-experienced tester pressed the search key at every wall, sometimes several times, Ultimate ADOM now discovers secret doors automatically when the player moves close. Players still have to visit the relevant areas, but they no longer rely on luck, and Biskup expects similar treatment for traps ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 29:02](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1742)).

Traps are the clearest test of partial disclosure. Joris Dormans argues that completely hidden traps never become interesting: the player should always know that something in the dungeon has changed, even if its exact nature is unclear, and the more of a trap you can expose without revealing all of it, the more interesting it gets ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 31:50](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1910)). Reed Lockwood offers a toolkit for doing that. Passive clues: treasure as bait (why is that item lying in the middle of the floor?), remains of earlier victims, messages about a smell or a draft, blood, bones, soot, or a suspiciously clean patch in a fungus-coated floor where a trap has already fired ([Reed Lockwood 2022, 8:16](https://youtu.be/ymgmhtkRLyY?t=496)). Active detection: let thrown items trigger traps, which he says seems obvious but is not often implemented, or give limited-use items such as chalk dust that reveal tripwires or vents ([Reed Lockwood 2022, 8:42](https://youtu.be/ymgmhtkRLyY?t=522)).

**In practice.** For each mechanic, decide which of the four routes the player will take to understand it:

- **Common-sense mapping** where your fiction is close to everyday experience and you can afford to honour the expectation everywhere.
- **In-world cue** (clothing, architecture, flavour text, a clean patch of floor) where you want reading the world to be the skill.
- **Explicit statement** (stats, recall, a knowledge menu) where the decision matters and a wrong guess would feel arbitrary. You can state what matters without stating how much.
- **Partial hint** where the fun is in the last step of inference: show one component of the hazard, describe the item as "sticky", and let the player finish the thought.

What you should not do is leave a mechanic in none of these categories, so that the only route to it is luck or an outside source.

## Known and unknown: information as a design lever

Every roguelike decides what the player knows and what they do not, even in its most basic limit, which Jonathan Lessard defends as deliberate: the player's awareness extends only to their own view of the game ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 3:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=189)). The talks treat this as a dial. You can hide goals, costs or outcomes separately, and which one you hide changes what kind of game you have, as Nic Tringali's The Banished Vault shows by revealing every resource and hiding only the cost ([Nic Tringali 2023, 17:51](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1071)).

### The deck is already shuffled

Nic Tringali offers a useful way to think about it. An unexplored dungeon or a branching story works like a shuffled deck: the information already exists and the game knows it. Uncertainty exists only from the player's point of view, and each step collapses a small slice of an already-decided reality. The player can wait as long as they like but can only learn or respond after the fact; the risk is how far in they dare to go, as when trying to romance a party member through a conversation tree ([Nic Tringali 2026, 4:59:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17997)).

> When you enter a dungeon and you can't see around the corner, the game knows what's there. — [Nic Tringali 2026, 4:59:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=17997)

His own game, The Banished Vault, turns the usual arrangement inside out. On arrival in a system the player sees every resource on the map; there are no secret or surprise resources, the manual says how much of each a building needs, and the fuel cost of any trip can be calculated exactly ([Nic Tringali 2023, 15:05](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=905)). What stays uncertain is the cost: hazard results, a semi-randomised grid, mutually exclusive resource tiles where building on one precludes the other, and resource depth that requires excavators. Tringali sums up the model as the player knowing what they will get but not at what cost ([Nic Tringali 2023, 17:51](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1071)).

That changes what exploration is. In The Banished Vault exploring means choosing a route through chaotic but known information, not uncovering new information; players may spend 10 to 30 minutes on the map before making a move, because the information is finite but too broad to grasp at once. Tringali stresses that this only works because the game tells players where their goals are ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:49](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1249)). He goes further: he wants players' plans to be flawed. The truest uncertainty, in his account, is the player's own doubt about whether they have considered every possibility, followed by the mistakes they make carrying the plan out ([Nic Tringali 2023, 21:32](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1292)). And he argues the reverse design would fail: with the time pressure and the physicality of resources, hiding resource locations would make the game too hard and unfair, feeling like output randomness (luck that strikes after the decision) even though it is not ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:56](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1256)).

### Building play out of what is hidden

Other designs put the hidden information at the centre. In The Shrouded Isle every villager has one virtue and one vice tied to the cult's five values, and discovering those traits is the core puzzle; players make educated guesses to find and purge sinners. Cat Manning points out the tension this creates: the characters you have investigated most, and who have therefore become most interesting, are the ones you must sacrifice ([Cat Manning 2020, 13:51](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=831)). Jongwoo Kim argues that hidden information here rewards prudence and foresight: skilled players learn to make reasonable assumptions and rely on less and less information, while the need for information pushes everyone to get to know the characters, and it leaves room for good intentions to go wrong ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 20:28](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1228)). Where Tringali argues that hidden goals would feel unfair, Kim makes hidden traits the skill test, with the inquiry system described above as the safety valve.

Smaller doses of concealment shape decisions elsewhere. Bruno Dias gives the player a few possible next destinations in Voyageur with only one or two facts about each, so the player juggles several interests and a rumour is more likely to be relevant to them; he lists this limited information as one of three mechanics, with procedural generation and forward motion, that produce serendipity ([Bruno Dias 2016, 14:22](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=862)). Francesco Cottone's printed game Chronicles of Stampadia tracks the player's decisions with a shuffled set of checkboxes, one per room, which obscures the consequences of choices from the very player who ticks them ([Francesco Cottone 2021, 9:31](https://youtu.be/IPMXeSAvtDs?t=571)). Jonathan Lessard defends the genre's most basic limit, that the player's awareness extends only to their view of the game, as a deliberate and valid choice, while noting its price: everything outside attention and everything in the past is lost ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 3:09](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=189)). And in the 2016 lightning talks Sean Mayne pointed to Diplomacy's secret simultaneous moves as a reminder that hidden information is an alternative to dice for creating uncertainty ([Tariq et al. 2016, 4:30](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=270)).

### Concealment as texture

Hiding can also be a moment-to-moment effect rather than a structure:

- Brogue's hallucination hides monster identities. Qristy Overton's player, licked by a toad, chose to fight an unknown creature and died to a jackal that had appeared as a unicorn ([Qristy Overton 2021, 14:50](https://youtu.be/zlJNIJOog9M?t=890)).
- Jamie Brew's Robot Karaoke has a flashcard mode that hides each Balatro card name until after it should have been sung, so the singer must recall it from memory ([Jamie Brew 2025, 18:05](https://youtu.be/685wpSUVw9s?t=1085)).
- Joe Sondow found that followers of Emoji Meadow particularly enjoy camouflaged green animals, a turtle or a snake that is hard to spot, which turn a tweet into a small puzzle ([Joe Sondow 2017, 6:01](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=361)).
- Everest Pipkin catalogues games that bury treasure and give the player indirect senses for it: dowsing in Pokémon, smelling in a Yoshi game, metal detectors, and Sea of Thieves's treasure maps found in the world or made by other players ([Everest Pipkin 2026, 10:00](https://youtu.be/VwZS0MQSpaU?t=600)).

**In practice.** Decide separately what the player knows about three things: the **goals** (what is out there to get), the **costs** (what it will take) and the **outcomes** (what happens when they act). Then hide the one whose uncertainty makes the decision interesting. Tringali shows everything but the cost and gets long planning sessions ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:49](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1249)); Kim hides the traits that decide outcomes and gets inference about people ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 20:28](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1228)). If you hide something, check what the player can do to learn it, and whether its absence will read as skill or as luck ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:56](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1256); [Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)).

## System suspense: designing the unknown on purpose

The sections so far mostly argue for legibility. This one presents the strongest case for deliberately keeping parts of a game unknown, and the conditions under which that works.

### What system suspense is

Alexei Pepers presents system suspense, a term from the Caves of Qud team that she credits to Jason Grinblat's blog post "Apologia for Game Wikis", as the experience of moving through game systems that do not make their boundaries known, where players discover the axioms themselves and learning the game is part of the fun. Her Caves of Qud examples: dominating a snapjaw shows its inventory, a cave spider has pseudopods, and spraying a door with "spray-a-brain" lets you dominate a now-sentient door and equip it, which makes players wonder what the game is even capable of ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 5:17](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=317)).

She defines it against surprise. The player's mental model is their understanding of how the game links together, a surveyed map of what is inside and outside it. Surprise is a sudden change in that model; suspense is a lingering awareness that part of it is fuzzy and cannot yet be resolved. To design suspense you shape the mental model on purpose and then draw the player's attention to the uncertainty ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 13:03](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=783)).

Her central practical claim is that the default instinct to remove uncertainty also removes the space for suspense and surprise. Working on Blaseball, which had many hard-to-understand elements, the team decided case by case where to preserve uncertainty and where to remove it.
