The distinction to draw is between productive uncertainty and unproductive uncertainty, not between clear and unclear ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 35:32](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2132)).

### The conditions: clarity everywhere else, cheap hypotheses

System suspense is not permission to be vague. Pepers insists that games built on it still need tutorials and very clear communication in the areas that are not meant to be mysterious, so the player has the cognitive space to test hypotheses about the parts that are. Dwarf Fortress now has a tutorial without losing its mysterious depth. If there is too much noise, or players do not know how to act on a hypothesis, they are not engaging with a fuzzy area; they are just lost ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057)).

> For the areas that are not meant to be suspenseful, make sure that they are very clear and well understood. — [Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057)

The second condition is cost. Suspense turns to frustration when testing a hypothesis is unfun, sits outside the core loop, or is expensive to get wrong. Her case is Baldur's Gate 3, which highlights mechanical keywords clearly elsewhere but hides secret affordances among junk: a shovel carrying only flavour text, like the sellable forks and spoons, lets you dig up a buried chest if it is in your inventory ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 19:04](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1144)). Discovering it makes players feel smart, but it also makes them hoard heavy junk in case it matters, and a "small shovel" does not dig; the developers eventually patched the shovel's description to state its use, judging the cost not worth it. Pepers links this directly to identification by use in roguelikes, which many modern roguelikes consider too punishing when it wastes valuable consumables ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 21:28](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1288)). (The identification section below takes this up.)

### Resolving uncertainty, or not

Pepers describes three ways to resolve a fuzzy area: a designed surprise that hits every player at one moment (Resident Evil 3's safe room breach); an ambient realisation each player reaches on their own (The Witness's environmental puzzles, powerful but some players bounce off first); or breadcrumbs in between (Tactical Breach Wizards' cosmetic optional objectives, which often require unintuitive system interactions and hint at what is possible without forcing it) ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 24:58](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1498)). She also argues, while granting it is counterintuitive, that some uncertainty never needs resolving: content players never see can still add value if they believe it existed and speculate about it. In Blaseball, the believable existence of unseen options fed the suspense ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 37:04](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2224)).

Her examples show suspense spreading from one discovery to the whole system. Mass Effect 2 ties the crew's survival to a hidden counter of missions completed after their abduction; when crew die because of wasted time, players realise the game tracks things it never surfaced and start asking what else it tracks and which of their assumptions are wrong ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 9:03](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=543)). FromSoftware games keep exploration suspenseful by having many secret-finding mechanics, each used only a few times, such as Dark Souls's illusory walls and Elden Ring's teleport trap that suddenly zooms the map out, and adding a few more in each game ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 45:15](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2715)). Caves of Qud itself is often vague; Ray notes that a Joppa recoiler's description does not say that it teleports you, and the community forms folk theories of how the game works that are not necessarily aligned with the real mechanics, which feeds a sense of heightened rather than literal reality ([Ray 2025, 7:51](https://youtu.be/rPhXTcVVJmo?t=471)).

### Why roguelikes are suited to it

Many runs give mystery room to work. Arvi Teikari says that because roguelite players do many runs, Noita did not have to show everything in one: it could hide rare, obscure material interactions in the world, and a player who tries something random and sees something new reports it to others, which makes the game feel mysterious ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 26:16](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1576)). Because players are expected to experiment, the team could also leave the depth of wand building for players, or wikis, to find; Teikari calls this maybe controversial and admits it reduced the team's workload ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 27:55](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1675)). Courtney Liessen finds a related delight in rules: genre and franchise tropes make players assume certain rules are fixed, and revealing that one, such as an action RPG's damage conversion equation, can be changed delights them and makes them wonder what else they can make their own ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 4:53](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=293)).

Liessen also names the cost of making that discovery easy. Asked whether explicitly marking which rules players may edit loses something, she agreed there is a trade-off: signposting brings these stories to players who would never spend a hundred hours learning to exploit systems, but it gives up some of the roguelike pleasure of finding the unexpected yourself ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 14:48](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=888)). This is the same choice Pepers frames as productive versus unproductive uncertainty, seen from the accessibility side.

### The deliberately misleading game

A few speakers go past concealment to active misdirection. Leonard Richardson asks for more games that create mystery by misleading the player about their mechanics, either by keeping things secret or through an unreliable narrator, along with games whose fun comes from variety of content rather than tactics. He notes the genre has moved away from these Rogue and NetHack elements and asks designers to find the fun in neglected ideas even if they were neglected for good reason ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 12:10](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=730)). His own robotfindskitten is built on the ambiguity of roguelike symbols, finding fun in touching characters to discover what they are; he does not claim to like the ambiguity of whether a lowercase c is a cockatrice or a cat, only that it is a mystery exclusive to roguelikes ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 5:59](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=359)).

Joseph Hewitt brings in stage magic: misdirection lets you set up a reveal by getting players used to a rhythm and then breaking it, as Undertale does by presenting itself as a normal JRPG ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 9:30](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=570)). He adds that while games usually give players all the information, designers can sometimes obscure mechanics so things do not go the way the player assumes ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 10:00](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=600)). Paul Dean points to the novel Pale Fire, whose unreliable narrator lets readers discover for themselves that they are being lied to and flip back to check, the kind of figuring-out he says roguelike players love ([Paul Dean 2025, 16:19](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=979)).

**In practice.**

- Choose where uncertainty lives. Name the few systems whose boundaries you want players to probe, and treat uncertainty anywhere else as a bug.
- Make everything outside those areas crystal clear, including a tutorial if needed, so players have attention to spare for the mystery.
- Make hypotheses cheap to test: inside the core loop, quick, and not ruinous when wrong.
- Decide how each fuzzy area resolves: a designed surprise, an ambient realisation, or breadcrumbs. Some may never resolve, and that can be fine if players believe something is there.
- Spread secrets thinly across many runs and many mechanics, so the suspense attaches to the system as a whole rather than to one trick.

## Identification: the per-run puzzle of unknown items

Item identification, where potions, scrolls and wands have randomised appearances each run and their effects must be discovered, is the genre's founding discovery mechanic. It is also where the chapter's tensions are sharpest, because the same mechanic reads as a puzzle to some players and as a chore to others ([Lisa Brown 2020, 25:37](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1537)).

### Why it exists, and the case against it

Santiago Zapata traces it to Rogue's limitations. Rogue was in the end a simple game, and having to identify potions, wands and scrolls made a small fixed content set feel larger, as if the Dungeon Master were inventing new magic items each game ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 11:13](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=673)).

The case against it is made most strongly by Thomas Biskup, who removed identification by default from Ultimate ADOM. The fun, he argues, should be in discovering interesting uses of items, and if you must identify almost everything before understanding it you lose much of the fun of interactions. Casual players did not understand identification, and hunting for scrolls was tedium; a hardcore mode might bring it back ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 13:16](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=796)). Identification surprised the team in testing along with the deadly hunger system and statistical notation, and the goal of removing it was behavioural: players should use items when they find them instead of dying with unused items in their backpack ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1064)).

> We wanted people to use the items when they find them, not just die with unused items in their backpack. — [Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1064)

Slay the Spire reached a similar decision for different reasons. Casey Yano recalls that it originally had traditional unidentified potions that you used to identify and could combine, but potion drops were infrequent and the screen already had many items on it, so the mechanic did not last long into beta-style playtesting ([Casey Yano 2022, 6:49](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=409)). Lisa Brown, whose preference for exposed rules was described under who is learning, found original Rogue's unidentified potions and scrolls and combat-learned enemy capabilities tiring work, though she would recommend it to players who score high on discovery motivation ([Lisa Brown 2020, 25:37](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1537)). Pepers's warning about costly hypothesis tests, in the system suspense section, is the general form of all three complaints.

### Making it a game rather than a chore

The defenders of identification describe ways of narrowing the possibilities that are themselves interesting:

- **Price identification.** In Adeon's NetHack speedrun, commentators explain that each item type has a fixed shop price that scales with charisma but stays proportional, so a shop's price narrows which scroll, potion, boots or lamp an item might be. Adeon names a scroll "ID" from its price without ever reading it, and later tells a magic lamp from an oil lamp by price and elimination ([Adeon 2017, 5:44](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=344)). Robin Mendoza suggests prices could do more in this mini-game: confirm a legendary item's provenance, or signal that someone is dumping a cursed item cheaply ([Robin Mendoza 2024, 4:33](https://youtu.be/ZtXGg6ECwQ8?t=273)).
- **Distinctive test actions.** NetHack lets players identify many wands by engraving with them, since each type produces a distinctive message: magic missile leaves the floor "riddled with bullets", digging throws up gravel and leaves a permanent engraving. It costs a charge but tells far more than zapping wands at a wall ([Adeon 2017, 18:23](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=1103)).
- **Bigger pools.** Eric Billingsley, working within Pico-8's tiny item budget for Into Ruins, merged categories: one pool of eight differently coloured orbs takes longer to narrow down than two pools of four. Orbs also probe the world; throwing an orb of data, normally used to identify equipment, at a goblin reveals its name and stats ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 19:37](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1177)).
- **Partly fixed, partly random associations.** Spencer Egart, designing generated ritual spells, mixes fixed intuitive mappings (a fire rune means fire, since fire meaning water would be incomprehensible) with per-run randomised ones (made-up runes reassigned to elements each run). A player who knows the fire blessing and learns which rune means water can substitute runes to derive a parallel ritual ([Spencer Egart 2019, 7:28](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=448)).

How much the identification game matters depends on how cheaply the player can bypass it. John Harris notes that in Advanced Rogue 5 the classes do not play very differently, except that a high-intelligence magician who starts with an identify spell completely changes the nature of the game, because casting identify from memory removes the risk of testing unknown items ([John Harris 2021, 15:28](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=928)). A single starting ability can switch the whole mechanic off.

### Frontiers and readings

Mike Cook sees unidentified potions as an existing case of procedurally generated rules whose novelty fades once players learn the effects and the detection techniques. He proposes supercharging the idea by generating the mechanics themselves, so the potions stay fresh ([Mike Cook 2023, 10:18](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=618)). Alexandra Leonhart reads the mechanic through Foucault's idea of power/knowledge: each run's hidden rule set defines what is true (the orange potion may be healing or fire), and the player can drink, throw or ignore it but has agency only within the rule set established for that run ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:10:04](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29404)).

The trope is familiar enough to be played with outside games. Zack Johnson describes Kingdom of Loathing's NetHack-themed zone, whose potions used NetHack's adjectives with effects randomised per player ([Zack Johnson 2016, 21:51](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1311)). A Dungeon Court case put a wizard on trial for handing his ally an unidentified potion that turned her into a rat unable to carry her treasure; the judge ordered them to split and both drink the next five unknown potions ([Randy Lubin and Raph D'Amico 2019, 40:25](https://youtu.be/ftSC3Sn8O_s?t=2425)). Dustin Freeman's live-action roguelike reproduces the risk directly: drinking an unknown pink potion turns the player into a tree and ends the run, and later items are learned by use while many go unused and unidentified ([Dustin Freeman 2023, 4:48](https://youtu.be/mXRKvbRi9qc?t=288)).

**In practice.** If you keep identification, make it cheap to probe (tests inside normal play that do not burn your best consumables), rich in partial clues (prices, messages, fixed intuitive anchors among the randomised ones) and short enough to finish within a run, so items get used rather than carried to the grave ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1064); [Adeon 2017, 18:23](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=1103); [Spencer Egart 2019, 7:28](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=448)). Watch for any ability that trivialises it, and decide whether that is a class feature or a hole ([John Harris 2021, 15:28](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=928)). If you remove it, know what you lose: the sense of a larger content set ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 11:13](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=673)) and the per-run puzzle that some of your players come for.

## Clues, riddles and research: discovery as investigation

Discovery does not have to be accidental. Several talks describe games where the game holds the answers and the player's job is to find and assemble them, like a researcher or a detective ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 20:52](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1252); [Tarn Adams 2018, 19:40](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1180)). The design questions are how clues reach the player, how much the game should flag them, and how to keep the puzzle fair.

### The game as archive

Jason Grinblat built Caves of Qud's library to evoke sifting through tattered tomes. A player can take a north-south secret from one generated book and cross-reference it with an east-west secret from another to narrow a pistol's location to a single world-map tile, nine maps, an area small enough to explore ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 20:52](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1252)). Qud's generated history works the same way at a larger scale. Unlike Dwarf Fortress's legends mode, Qud never exposes the history directly; players learn it only through artifacts in the present-day world, such as shrines to sultans, an engraved mace showing a sultan's birth or wine bottles painted with scenes, all of which are ordinary usable items that can also be examined ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 4:13](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=253)).

Grinblat is also relaxed about bad information in the archive. Books generated by Markov chains from NPC dialogue rarely produce plausible but wrong secrets, since false statements tend to be obviously absurd, and he likes some misinformation as long as it does not look too much like the right answer ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 26:32](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1592)).

### Cryptic riddles and unflagged leads

Mark Johnson's model is the cryptic riddle. In La-Mulana's gem-scales puzzle, the player must combine clues seen hours apart: tablets giving gem colours and weights, a clue mentioning sapphire, and a hidden pair of scales reporting the player's own weight in the game's fictional language, decoded by toggling auto-translation and comparing numerals, before splitting gems and player to balance at 244 per side ([Mark Johnson 2023, 3:43](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=223)). What makes such puzzles compelling, he argues, is that each demands a new kind of attention to the world (maths, the game's language, the map, room names, NPC dialogue, obscure room details) rather than iterating one puzzle type over and over; he cites Riven, Fez, Environmental Station Alpha, Outer Wilds and Tunic ([Mark Johnson 2023, 8:51](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=531)). In Ultima Ratio Regum he refuses to flag leads with quest markers or logs. A generated holy book mentions two saints who left sacred pottery at meditation spots, and nothing tells you to follow up, because noticing something yourself and trusting that the game will reward following it is more rewarding ([Mark Johnson 2023, 11:23](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=683)).

Tarn Adams finds that investigation falls out of a simulation when the player knows only what is local. A player who arrives in a Dwarf Fortress village with no knowledge of a hidden villain network can learn by talking about the murders, the necromancer, the ruler and the elf war, but not the threads connecting them, which naturally becomes a step-by-step mystery ([Tarn Adams 2018, 19:40](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1180)). Because the game knows the actual plot, townspeople can feed the player an arbitrary amount of hints about what they have not yet found, giving a tunable difficulty control ([Tarn Adams 2018, 22:40](https://youtu.be/4-7TtPX5uhg?t=1360)).

Older and odder examples show the same pattern. Jeff Olson's Alphaman required thought rather than just tech weapons to beat its final boss: in-game computers gave clues to each castle's secret, including that the Grinch has a soft spot for roast beef ([Jeff Olson 2023, 16:19](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=979)). In Bad News, where a player investigates a death by talking to a live actor, players take a lot of notes (which the team encourages), look up the body's address in the directory to find the deceased's surname, and commonly start at a bar or diner because approaching people at home after role-playing feels awkward ([Bad News team 2016, 18:40](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=1120)). Face-to-face conversation also raises tension: the actor pushes back if the player leaves mid-conversation to look things up, so players feel they need to be prepared, and time that seems slow to spectators passes quickly for them ([Bad News team 2016, 46:55](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=2815)).

### Fairness: obtuse but not unfair

Paris Buttfield-Addison's Hintline 93, a museum exhibit about 1993 game hint lines, had to invent puzzles hard enough that a player would pay by the minute for help. The team's rule was that they be "obtuse but not unfair": rationally solvable with enough time. One is a temporal lock that needs you to stand exactly two steps from a door for five seconds during a green light phase, with a clue in the rhythm of the lights ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:24:06](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23046)). Its hint system copies what good counsellors did: they asked where you were stuck and what you had tried, so you felt you had solved it yourself, and the game's hint button likewise points to where to look rather than giving the answer ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:19:49](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=22789)). Its compendium deliberately includes wrong official guidance, like the real hint lines' mistranslated or early-version documentation, so players must check sources against each other. Buttfield-Addison compares NetHack, where the Oracle's rumours are always true but fortune-cookie rumours can be false ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:25:51](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23151)). Grinblat's tolerance for obviously absurd misinformation and Buttfield-Addison's flagged-as-wrong guide are two versions of the same rule: unreliable sources are fine if the player has a way to tell.

Andrew Plotkin's talk on mazes turns into a set of fairness rules for any investigation. A purely decorative maze with no reward is a red herring: players will hunt for a secret that is not there, so it must be clearly labelled as artistic or players get annoyed. He values puzzle games where every element turns out to have a purpose; a good experience is searching for something that is there and finding it ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 20:33](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=1233)). Even a single-path labyrinth with no branches feels like a maze because following it takes work and you can lose your place, which is a form of getting lost ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 12:37](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=757)). Colossal Cave's maze has no landmarks, so players drop items and draw maps; Zork's thief then moves the items you dropped, deliberately breaking the player's toolkit, and Plotkin says every adventure game of that era tried a new way to mess with the player's head ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 16:33](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=993)). Finally, a rule maze becomes a rule-discovery puzzle if you withhold the rule: given a colour maze without its sequence, a player can reason that only red-blue-yellow makes it neither trivial nor too hard, and that deduced sequence can then serve as a clue elsewhere. He cites The Witness and Zero Player and admits a hidden right-turn rule might be too hard for most players ([Andrew Plotkin 2026, 24:15](https://youtu.be/7h3T5NaFpcI?t=1455)).

Bjarke Alexander Larsen's Discord logic puzzle, Corrupted Databases, shows two ways an investigation can fail. With five similar databases, all mapping name to address or address to name, players could query all of them and pick the most frequent answer; this became the dominant strategy and playtesters found it boring ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 8:50](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=530)). And the real problem was not how many puzzles were truly unsolvable but how many players perceived as impossible, because feeling that a puzzle is impossible makes players quit exactly as if it were ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 14:27](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=867)).

> Feeling like it's impossible and it being impossible then often becomes the same thing. — [Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 14:27](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=867)

**In practice.**

- Every clue should lead somewhere, and everything that looks like a puzzle should be one, or be labelled clearly as decoration.
- Let clues require different kinds of attention, and let them be found far apart.
- If you include unreliable sources, give the player a way to sort them, and keep false answers from looking like true ones.
- Check that no simple strategy (query everything, take the majority) short-circuits the reasoning.
- Solvability must be felt, not only true: give the player reasons to believe progress is possible, and consider hints that say where to look rather than what the answer is, ideally tunable because the game knows what has not been found.

## Spoilers, wikis and the solved game

Every roguelike that lasts acquires a body of knowledge outside itself: wikis, FAQs, spoiler files, strategy guides. This is the chapter's sharpest disagreement. Some designers see outside knowledge as a threat to design against ([Brian Walker 2016, 3:18](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=198)); others see it as part of the game's culture, or as discovery in its own right ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163)).

### The threat: rote play and lazy design

Brian Walker states the strongest version of the worry. The biggest risk to a game's longevity is play becoming rote, where the player immediately knows the answer to every situation, as with tic-tac-toe once you memorise its solution tree. The internet makes it worse, because players do not even build the intuition themselves; they alt-tab to a wiki mid-game, so designers must make systems resistant to crowdsourced data dumps ([Brian Walker 2016, 3:18](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=198)). He ties this to a principle he credits the Crawl team with popularising and calls the most important aspect of game design: optimal play should be fun. Looking up the dominant strategy or each item's effect is optimal play that is not fun, and you have to account for it ([Brian Walker 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=280)).

Several designers put the same point as a rule about where knowledge must live. Thomas Biskup says mechanics should be deducible from in-game observation and that requiring FAQs or spoilers is lazy design, which he admits ADOM is guilty of ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955)). Andrew Aversa says a wiki is not bad in itself (Tangledeep has one) but needing it open to have any chance of winning is a sign of bad difficulty; the more the game presents itself, the better ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 3:43](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=223)). George Moromisato warns that combinatorial complexity risks "guide dang it" design, the TV Tropes term for mechanics whose solution can only be looked up, though he finds NetHack minimises it more than one might expect ([George Moromisato 2016, 13:48](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=828)). Jim Shepard says roguelike bosses should not require learning by repeated death as MMO raids do, nor require spoilers, though spoilers can optionally reveal broken builds for those who want them; he admits Dungeonmans has some near-mandatory spoiler content and that he did a bad job there ([Jim Shepard 2017, 31:41](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1901)). His summary is that players should never need to go online to work out how to progress ([Jim Shepard 2017, 32:34](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1954)).

### The defence: encyclopedias, not cheat sheets

Jeremy Rose disputes the premise. Treating wikis and spoiler guides as cheating is, he says, an impoverished view: they are encyclopedias that inform rather than prescribe (an encyclopedia tells you bleach is corrosive, not that you should avoid drinking it), and browsing them is itself discovery. He cites studies finding that spoilers increase enjoyment, and notes there has been only a single unspoiled NetHack ascension: are all the others false victories ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163))?

His Hitchhiker's Guide to the Cataclysm puts this into practice by making every relationship between the game's nouns visible and bidirectional. Duct tape's page shows every recipe that uses it and every way to obtain it, including crafting from thread, super glue and cotton patches, rare monster drops, or deconstructing a taped window. Seeing that deconstructing terrain yields items prompts players to wonder what else they could get that way, such as a sheet of glass, so the guide surfaces possibilities players did not think to look for ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 11:42](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=702)). Because Cataclysm changes constantly, players keep meeting new things anyway, and the guide makes a few careful omissions ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163)).

Others defend outside knowledge more modestly. Drew Streib, who co-hosts the NetHack wiki, argues that being spoiled does not ruin NetHack: knowing what will happen does not save you when you make the wrong choice, and many fully spoiled players still cannot win ([Drew Streib 2016, 25:22](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1522)). Max Kreminski thinks designers worry too much about players spoiling generated stories through wikis; players who strategise from spoilers affect only their own experience, enough storylets can outlast their interest, and the main approach is not to fight it ([Max Kreminski 2017, 19:31](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1171)). Jason Grinblat goes furthest. Caves of Qud's Joppa massacre bug teaches players about important systems by pushing them to the wiki and community discussion; he knows that is anathema to modern design ethos but thinks it can be good, though he calls the decision whether to fix it "even money" and the fix already sits commented out in the data ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 20:43](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1243)).

What the choice depends on is visible in the positions themselves. Walker, Biskup and Aversa are worried about required lookups that replace play ([Brian Walker 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=280); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 3:43](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=223)); Rose and Streib are describing lookups that inform play the player still has to execute ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163); [Drew Streib 2016, 25:22](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1522)), and Kreminski does not think fighting them is worth it ([Max Kreminski 2017, 19:31](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1171)). A spoiler that tells you the answer to every situation makes the game rote ([Brian Walker 2016, 3:18](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=198)); one that tells you what exists still leaves you to decide and act ([Drew Streib 2016, 25:22](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1522)).

### What fighting spoilers costs

If you do want to resist outside knowledge, the talks warn that it cannot be beaten outright. John Harris concluded that no game can be made spoiler-proof; randomness only delays it. A NetHack walkthrough cannot read like an Elder Scrolls one, yet NetHack still has FAQs listing every possible item, and a game that invented its own items would get a FAQ on the limits of its range ([John Harris 2016, 22:09](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=1329)). Zack Johnson describes Kingdom of Loathing randomising puzzles and mazes to defeat wiki lookups; it interested the designers more than the players, who wrote Greasemonkey scripts to solve them automatically, which is effectively the same as looking them up, and the team has backed off ([Zack Johnson 2016, 20:48](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=1248)).

Randomisation works better when it is paired with an in-game source. Grinblat describes how Caves of Qud generates disease cures each game and records them in an in-game book, so players consult the book rather than the wiki ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 9:05](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=545)). The wiki can say where to look; only the game can say what this run's answer is. Walker's own conclusion is similarly modest: a richer, more contingent strategy space cannot defeat wikis but tips the odds in the game's favour, in a competition with the metagame that can never be decisively won, and he is happy the Brogue wiki exists ([Brian Walker 2016, 27:44](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=1664)).

### A middle ground: decide what is looked up

Paris Buttfield-Addison reframes spoilers through hint lines, which sold by the minute the same knowledge roguelike players trade in spoiler files, because in a roguelike you are expected to die and what carries over is what you know. Roguelikes even contain hint lines: NetHack's Oracle sells minor and major consultations priced by experience level, and some players play pacifist to save gold for it ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:17:24](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=22644)).

> You're expected to die and what carries over to the next run is what you know. — [Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:17:24](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=22644)

From this he draws a test. Some NetHack deaths you can work out for yourself; the cockatrice corpse is one you look up after the first time it kills you. A designer can decide which deaths players should have to look up, and then make sure the answer exists somewhere in the game ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:24:46](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23086)).

Outside knowledge also has a shelf life. Erik Osheim and Robert Au note that Angband's documentation lagged its changes, so new players still find a 1996 newbie guide prescribing rigid depth checkpoints such as having free action by a certain depth ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 18:35](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=1115)). And Nic Tringali, asked how to stop players optimising chance-based games, says players optimise the fun out when they have played too much, know the game too well, or the game has an ideal path through its systems; he thinks the answer depends too much on the specific design to give generally, and notes players can choose to be swept along by uncertainty instead ([Nic Tringali 2026, 5:13:52](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=18832)).

**In practice.**

- Choose which knowledge you expect players to find outside the game, and accept that some will.
- For each piece of it, put a path inside the game: an in-game book, a message, a monster recall entry, a hint that points where to look.
- Do not rely on randomisation alone to defeat lookups. It delays them, and scripts can undo it; pair it with an in-game record of this run's answer.
- Keep the strategy space contingent enough that looking things up informs a decision rather than making it, so that optimal play is still play.

## Tensions and open questions

**Should everything be learnable in a short loop?** The mainstream position is that a choice is only meaningful when the player knows what she is choosing and can see its immediate and longer-term results ([Sersa Victory 2022, 7:03](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=423)), and that heavy outcome randomness teaches the wrong lessons by punishing good plays ([Shawn Main 2017, 10:18](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=618)). Jeff Lait argues that hard-to-learn games which force unguided meta-learning are a valid design space, and that designers should sometimes break the "everything learnable in a quick loop" rule on purpose ([Jeff Lait 2025, 9:30](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=570); [Jeff Lait 2025, 14:21](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=861); [Jeff Lait 2025, 29:16](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1756)). Lait agrees that most games should stay easy to learn ([Jeff Lait 2025, 29:16](https://youtu.be/LQPGmxytTws?t=1756)). The choice depends on whether learning the long loop unaided is the experience you want to offer, and on how many players you are willing to lose before they get there.

**Paced complexity or deliberate overwhelm?** Magic's commons and Luck be a Landlord's rarity curve gate complexity ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 4:38](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=278); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 11:10](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=670)), explicit synergy callouts help newcomers ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 17:11](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1031)), and too many choice prompts break flow ([Sersa Victory 2022, 30:28](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1828)). Jon Perry says UFO 50 overwhelms players on purpose ([Jon Perry 2025, 42:29](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2549)), yet he still held back Mini and Max's microscopic scale to make it a reveal ([Jon Perry 2025, 15:06](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=906)). Overwhelm can be an aesthetic, but even its advocate paces the things he most wants players to notice.

**Is randomness something to master or a licence to relax?** Sersa Victory sees the struggle to master uncertainty as the centre of the traditional roguelike ([Sersa Victory 2022, 8:08](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=488)). Perry uses randomness in Lords of Vicenzo precisely so players need not optimise ([Jon Perry 2025, 41:09](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=2469)), and the roguelite panel describes audiences split between challenge seekers and players who want to relax and explore ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 37:40](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=2260)). Which you choose depends on which of those players you are designing for.

**How much should stay hidden?** Alexei Pepers, Arvi Teikari and Leonard Richardson make the case for deliberate mystery: productive uncertainty, rare interactions spread across many runs, and even misdirection ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 35:32](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2132); [Arvi Teikari 2021, 26:16](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=1576); [Leonard Richardson 2017, 12:10](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=730)). Thomas Biskup, Jim Shepard and Andrew Aversa want mechanics deducible or presented in the game ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:55](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=955); [Jim Shepard 2017, 32:34](https://youtu.be/FZn4NeQOcFE?t=1954); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 3:43](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=223)). The positions meet in Pepers's own conditions: mystery works when everything else is clear and testing a hypothesis is cheap ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 17:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1057); [Alexei Pepers 2025, 21:28](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1288)). It also depends on who is playing; a low-discovery player like Lisa Brown wants rules exposed up front ([Lisa Brown 2020, 24:23](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1463)).

**Hidden goals: unfair luck or a skill test?** Nic Tringali argues that hiding resource locations in The Banished Vault would feel like unfair output randomness ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:56](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1256)); Jongwoo Kim makes hidden villager traits The Shrouded Isle's skill test ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 20:28](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1228)). What decides it in these two games is whether the player can investigate: Kim's inquiry system reveals why an outcome happened ([Jongwoo Kim 2018, 23:43](https://youtu.be/oV5PjvcVky8?t=1423)), while Tringali's design depends on players being told where their goals are ([Nic Tringali 2023, 20:49](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=1249)).

**Signposting or the pleasure of finding it yourself?** Courtney Liessen leaves this open: marking which rules players may edit brings rule-breaking to players who would never spend a hundred hours on it, but gives up some of the joy of discovering it unaided ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 14:48](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=888)). No talk resolves the trade-off.

**Identification: puzzle or chore?** It made Rogue's small content set feel larger ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 11:13](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=673)), and some players come for it ([Lisa Brown 2020, 25:37](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1537)); Biskup removed it from Ultimate ADOM because casual players found it tedious and died with unused items ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 13:16](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=796); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1064)). Pepers names the cost of probing as what turns it from game to chore ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 21:28](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=1288)), and cheap, informative tests exist ([Adeon 2017, 18:23](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=1103); [Adeon 2017, 5:44](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=344)).

**Fight the wiki or embrace it?** Brian Walker warns that lookups make play rote and that optimal play must stay fun ([Brian Walker 2016, 3:18](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=198); [Brian Walker 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=280)); Jeremy Rose, Drew Streib and Max Kreminski defend outside knowledge as encyclopedia, as insufficient to win, or as not worth fighting ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 19:23](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1163); [Drew Streib 2016, 25:22](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1522); [Max Kreminski 2017, 19:31](https://youtu.be/66O6WDcT8KY?t=1171)). Jason Grinblat sits on both sides, moving disease cures into an in-game book to keep players off the wiki ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 9:05](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=545)) while defending a bug that sends them to it ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 20:43](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1243)). This chapter's reading, which is an editorial synthesis rather than any speaker's claim, is that the split is between lookups that replace play and lookups that inform it.

**Open problems.**

- What happens when the knowledge runs out? John Harris found that NetHack's depth is finite once you have read the wiki enough ([John Harris 2016, 4:31](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=271)), and Tringali thinks how to stop players optimising the fun out depends too much on the specific design to answer generally ([Nic Tringali 2026, 5:13:52](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=18832)).
- Can discovery carry a game on its own? slashie's Expedition suggests it is hard to make exploration the main reason to return ([slashie 2026, 9:09:23](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32963)).
- Several promising techniques are untested by their proposers: Alex Byaly's week-long fixed correlations ([Alex Byaly 2022, 25:03](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1503)), bhauth's archetype video tutorials and unlockable mid-game saves ([bhauth 2020, 21:01](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1261)), and Mike Cook's suggestion that designers map their own play to see what they attend to ([Mike Cook 2026, 20:10](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1210)).
- How do you find out what players actually learned? Gillian Smith suggests borrowing ungrading from teaching ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:17:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4652)), but Max Sahin warns that asking players about their experience yields little ([Max Sahin 2025, 1:46](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=106)).

## Checklist

1. What is your game meant to teach, and have you written it down as a list of rules, judgements and habits?
2. How does an expert play differently from a novice, and can a player cross each part of that gap from inside the game?
3. Where does knowledge accumulate: only in the player's head, or also in an in-game record such as a monster memory or knowledge menu?
4. Can a player perceive the structure of your generators, or do some inputs and techniques leave no visible signature?
5. Do your random rolls use shaped distributions where you want players to strategise, and could an early streak teach a false rule?
6. For each long-term habit the game demands, when does the player first get evidence that it matters, and is that early enough?
7. Does death explain itself: who or what did the damage, from where, and what the player could have done instead?
8. Which genre conventions does your game assume, and which have you chosen to rely on, teach or subvert?
9. Have you watched newcomers play, rather than asking them how they felt?
10. Is every explicit tutorial limited to foundations that are not fun to discover, and does extra help reach only players who are struggling?
11. How is complexity paced: by rarity, by gating whole systems, by calling out obvious synergies, by limiting how often you ask for decisions?
12. For each mechanic, is the route to understanding it common sense, an in-world cue, an explicit statement or a partial hint, and is any left to luck or a wiki?
13. Which uncertainties are deliberate, is everything else crystal clear, and are hypotheses about the deliberate ones cheap to test?
14. If you keep item identification, can players probe it cheaply and finish it within a run, and does any ability trivialise it?
15. Which knowledge do you expect players to look up outside the game, and is there a path to it inside?
